title: Hamzah, lion of Allah
hookLine: his uncle Hamzah, the lion of Allah, is killed at Uhud, and the Prophet ﷺ grieves

cards: Years before Medina, in Mecca, a big, proud hunter comes home from the desert, bow on his shoulder. A woman stops him: while you were gone, Abu Jahl insulted your nephew Muhammad to his face, and he said nothing back.
He walks straight into the gathering of Quraysh, finds Abu Jahl, and strikes him with his bow. Then, in front of everyone: I follow his religion too. Hit me back if you can.
That was Hamzah, uncle of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, and from that day, the biographers say, Quraysh thought twice about harming the Prophet.

teach.h: ASAD ALLAH — THE LION OF GOD.
teach.b: Hamzah ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib was the Prophet's uncle, but, the biographers say, close to him in age, and the two had been nursed by the same woman as babies. The Prophet called him his brother through nursing.
He was strong and fearless, and at Badr he fought at the front. People called him asad Allah, the lion of God. But at Uhud a man was watching for him.
Wahshi was an Abyssinian slave in Mecca, skilled with a short throwing spear. His master had promised him freedom if he killed Hamzah, whose sword had killed the master's uncle at Badr.
Wahshi told the story himself, years later, and it's kept in Sahih al-Bukhari.
He hid behind a rock, waited for Hamzah to pass, and threw. Hamzah fell. After the battle, his body was found mutilated.
The early biographers describe the Prophet standing over him in deep grief.

teach.h: NO ONE TO WEEP FOR HAMZAH.
teach.b: Back in Medina, he heard the women of the Ansar weeping for their dead, and said: but Hamzah has no women to weep for him. And the women of Medina came to his door to weep for Hamzah.
Tradition calls Hamzah the master of the martyrs, and his grave lies at the foot of Uhud. Now the hardest part. Years later, Wahshi became Muslim and came to the Prophet, who did not turn him away.
Bukhari says he asked one question: are you the one who killed Hamzah? Wahshi said it was as he'd been told. Then the Prophet said: can you keep your face out of my sight?

how: Pilgrims to Medina visit the graves of Hamzah and the martyrs of Uhud at the foot of the mountain, greeting them and praying for them, and many Muslims name their sons Hamzah.

o: the Prophet's uncle, called the lion of God
a companion who later led the Muslim armies
the Prophet's cousin who married his daughter

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.

s: Hamzah was much older than the Prophet
he was his uncle but close to him in age, and they were nursed by the same woman.
Wahshi later became Muslim and met the Prophet
the Prophet accepted him, and asked him to keep his face out of sight.
the story of Hamzah's death comes from Wahshi himself
he told it years later, and it's kept in Sahih al-Bukhari.

games.q: years after Uhud, the man who killed your uncle comes to you and becomes Muslim. what do you do?
o: accept him, and ask him to keep out of your sight.
embrace him as if nothing happened.
games.why: the Prophet accepted him, asked one question, then said: can you keep your face out of my sight? acceptance, and grief, both.

practice: Let a person come to mind who stood up when it cost them something: someone well-known, or someone only you know, a grandparent, a teacher, a friend who spoke up for you when nobody else would.
If they've died, let yourself miss them for a minute, the way the Prophet missed Hamzah, and if you pray, you can make du'a for them.

wordCard.voice: Hamzah. The Prophet's uncle and nursing brother, the lion of God, killed at Uhud and remembered as the master of the martyrs. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: the lion of God, the title given to Hamzah.

carryVoice: Your line: the lion fell. And the women of Medina came to weep for him. Day two hundred sixty-seven.
